video_title: Who Will Control the Next Financial System?
gist: Former CFTC chairman Chris Giancarlo, promoting his book The New Adventures of Crypto Dad, argues SBF-driven politics and a 'rogue' Gensler SEC failed to stop crypto, that TradFi (DTCC, Swift, banks) will move the whole financial system onto tokenized digital rails by 2040, and that the CFTC under Mike Selig is right to onshore perpetuals. His biggest worry is privacy: he calls the GENIUS Act's Bank Secrecy Act regime a surveillance mistake and the CBDC-vs-stablecoin privacy debate a false choice.

insights.claim: Giancarlo argues crypto was not a partisan issue through roughly the first year of the Biden administration and only became political after Sam Bankman-Fried's campaign-contribution scandal embarrassed Democrats.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Crypto policy risk is tied to political narratives, not inherent party ideology; it can de-politicize again.
insights.quote: It didn't become political until Sam Bankman freed.

insights.claim: Giancarlo says the Elizabeth Warren wing of the Democratic party responded to the SBF embarrassment by going on offense and becoming hostile to crypto rather than admitting it got too close to a fraudster.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Explains the 2022-2024 enforcement climate as defensive politics.

insights.claim: Giancarlo frames the shift in Washington as driven by SBF, then the election, and Fairshake PAC money, which 'woke up' senators and congressmen to crypto's political power.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Crypto lobbying money is now a durable political force shaping legislation.

insights.claim: Giancarlo hopes crypto is returning to a non-political footing because the party's activist wing has redirected its opposition to data centers and AI.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Political opposition may rotate from crypto onto AI infrastructure, easing crypto regulatory risk.
insights.quote: Now they've set their opposition to innovation to data centers and they've set their opposition to AI and maybe they'll leave crypto alone.

insights.claim: Giancarlo rejects the view that all Democrats oppose crypto, naming Kirsten Gillibrand and the new Maryland senator Angela Alsobrooks as constructive, and pins hostility specifically on Elizabeth Warren.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Bipartisan support for market-structure legislation is more available than headlines suggest.

insights.claim: Giancarlo claims Gary Gensler saw becoming Treasury Secretary in a second Biden term as running through Elizabeth Warren's support, which led him to become the 'prosecutor of crypto'.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Regulatory posture can be driven by individual career incentives rather than policy merit.

insights.claim: Giancarlo says the SEC under Gensler refused to work with Congress, refused to write rules, enabled debanking of crypto companies and executives, and abused Wells notices to stop firms doing business even with no intent to prosecute, calling the SEC 'rogue' for the last two years of the Biden administration.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Supports the case for accountability and codified limits on enforcement-by-regulation.
insights.quote: the norm breaking that took place at the SEC under Gary Gensler is unprecedented and and and needs to be held to account.

insights.claim: Giancarlo notes the Clarity market-structure bill passed the House but stalled in the Senate, so eight years after his 2018 Senate testimony the US still lacks the 'smart regulatory framework' he called for.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: US market-structure clarity remains the key unresolved regulatory catalyst.
insights.quote: here we are 8 years later and we still don't have that framework.

insights.claim: Giancarlo argues US bank lobbies have spent 40-50 years using Washington clout to resist every innovation, including interstate banking, chip credit cards and ATMs, by telling community banks 'the sky is falling'.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Bank lobby opposition to crypto legislation (e.g. Clarity) is a pattern, likely a short-term win and long-term loss.

insights.claim: Giancarlo says bank lobbying groups fought the Clarity bill, but banks coast to coast will eventually have to adopt tokenized deposits anyway, so resistance only delays the inevitable and hurts regional banks.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Regional banks that delay digital-rail adoption face competitive damage.
insights.quote: banks from coast to coast are eventually going to have to adopt tokenized deposits anyway.

insights.claim: Giancarlo says the parties most annoyed by the CFTC's 2017 approval of the first Bitcoin futures were Wall Street banks, which ran full-page ads and got the Futures Industry Association to lobby Congress to rein him in, because they were unprepared.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Incumbent opposition often reflects readiness, not risk; they later adopted the asset class.

insights.claim: Giancarlo says Elizabeth Warren positions herself as a friend of the little guy while her campaign contributions come from large banks.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Frames anti-crypto politics as aligned with incumbent bank interests.

insights.claim: Giancarlo argues the Gensler-era crackdown held back but did not stop digital-asset innovation, and the firms that persevered emerged stronger and are now among the leading firms.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Survivors of the 2022-2024 enforcement era have strengthened competitive positions.
insights.quote: the firms that persevere just got stronger.

insights.claim: Giancarlo says all major banks and infrastructure providers such as DTCC and Swift are now adopting the technology because it is more efficient, lower cost and more accurate in tracking collateral and money.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Institutional adoption is driven by cost/efficiency economics, making it durable.

insights.claim: Giancarlo believes crypto's roots are now too deep to be ripped up even if Elizabeth Warren were elected president.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Regime-change political risk to crypto is lower than in prior cycles.
insights.quote: the roots are going to be too deep in the ground to be ripped up

insights.claim: Giancarlo predicts that by 2040 the entire financial system will have moved from its analog state onto digital rails, distributed ledger technology and tokenization.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: A ~15-year multi-trillion-dollar migration timeline for tokenization infrastructure.
insights.quote: within the next 12 to 15 years by the year uh 2040 the entire financial system is going to be moved from its current analog state into digital rails

insights.claim: Giancarlo cites DTCC's tokenized collateral experiment, with over 50 of the most important financial institutions, as a key use case: collateral stays inside DTCC but in tokenized form on a distributed ledger, removing the need to fund hundreds of accounts.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Collateral mobility is the beachhead for institutional tokenization.

insights.claim: Giancarlo expects institutions to move tokenization from closed environments ('the zoo') into open networks ('the wild') once they experience the precision and cost savings.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Permissioned pilots may be a stepping stone to more open/public-chain settlement.
insights.quote: Now, let's take it out of the zoo. let let's take this into the wild and they're going to do it.

insights.claim: Giancarlo says as CEO of public company GFI Group, with shares held in street name, they were lucky to know who 30% of their investors were, and on-chain shares would give issuers direct proximity to investors, making tokenization demand-driven as well as supply-driven.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Issuer demand for shareholder visibility is an underappreciated driver of tokenized equities.
insights.quote: we were lucky if we knew who 30% of our investors were

insights.claim: Giancarlo compares the current stage of tokenization to US railroads in the 1840s-1880s, with only the first rail laid, and says the new digital system will be built on top of the analog one as DTCC still holds bearer bonds in a vault.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Expect long coexistence of legacy and tokenized rails; early innings.

insights.claim: Giancarlo argues the generational shift, a cohort that grew up trading game tokens, will force adoption because they have no patience for paper checks and branch banking.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Demographics are a structural tailwind for digital-native finance.

insights.claim: Giancarlo says the CFTC-regulated crypto futures market, eight years after it approved the first Bitcoin futures, is deep, liquid, transparent and well policed against fraud and manipulation.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Regulated derivatives venues have proven market-structure viability for crypto.

insights.claim: Giancarlo explains the CFTC typically delays self-certified lookalike products for a couple of months after greenlighting a new asset class while it builds surveillance, pattern recognition, analyst coverage and overseas-regulator information sharing.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Explains cadence of new crypto derivative listings (ETH, XRP, SOL futures, etc.).

insights.claim: Giancarlo argues the CFTC's unique market-surveillance expertise is a reason not to merge it with the SEC, and that it likely uncovers far more misbehavior than it publicizes.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Argues against SEC-CFTC merger proposals.

insights.claim: Giancarlo pushes back on the idea that perpetuals are a novel instrument: derivatives default to settlement dates because of agricultural growing cycles, and once the CFTC accepted financial futures in the 1970s rolling settlement became inevitable; the CFTC has never banned perps, only required retail access via a fully licensed DCM.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Onshore US perps face less regulatory friction than markets assume.
insights.quote: there's nothing that says you can't have a rolling settlement date with no final settlement.

insights.claim: Giancarlo credits CFTC Chairman Mike Selig with determination to bring perpetual futures onshore so US investors get US regulation instead of that of Singapore or the Philippines.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Expect a US onshore perps market to grow, competing with offshore venues.

insights.claim: Giancarlo uses the Eurodollar market as a cautionary tale: 1970s Fed caps on US deposit rates pushed dollars to London banks, making LIBOR the benchmark for US mortgages, showing bad policy pushes markets offshore.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Restrictive US rules on crypto risk ceding benchmark/market dominance offshore.
insights.quote: bad policy can sometimes force things to happen offshore.

insights.claim: Giancarlo says decentralized markets like Hyperliquid are a much bigger intellectual and policy chasm for the CFTC to cross than perpetual futures themselves.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: DeFi derivatives venues face the hardest unresolved US regulatory questions.
insights.quote: decentralized markets like Hyperlord are a much bigger uh intellectual and policy bridge or chasm to cross than our perpetuals.

insights.claim: Giancarlo argues US-invented financial futures (Richard Sandor, Leo Melamed in Chicago) enabled the US to leave the gold standard by letting dollar holders hedge rate and FX risk, underpinning 30 years of globalization.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Positions crypto derivatives as continuation of American financial-innovation leadership.

insights.claim: Giancarlo frames Dodd-Frank (2010) as Washington's victory over Wall Street, creating shared political/market control of capital allocation, which crypto challenges by replacing both with algorithmic protocols.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Crypto threatens a Washington-Wall Street duopoly over capital allocation, explaining incumbent resistance.
insights.quote: The DoddFrank Act passed in 2010 was the victory of Washington over Wall Street.

insights.claim: Giancarlo concludes the digital network future will be as complex as the analog past: a rough equilibrium between centralized power (major banks working with DTC) and decentralized power, with Bitcoin as the best example of decentralized capital allocation.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Expect hybrid outcomes: neither full decentralization nor full TradFi capture.
insights.quote: the digital network future is going to be as complex as the analog past.

insights.claim: Giancarlo uses the American Revolution as a model: a decentralized militia started it, a new centralized hierarchy (Continental Army) finished it, and the result was a government with both federal and local power centers.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Mental model for how crypto might end: re-hierarchized but with distributed power.

insights.claim: Giancarlo recounts that at GFI Group roughly two-thirds or more of the world's credit default swap market traded on its platforms, and weeks before Lehman fell he told the New York Fed that Lehman was 'already gone' because banks would not trade with it.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Counterparty-refusal signals precede formal failure.

insights.claim: Giancarlo says the Fed estimated $400B in gross CDS payouts on a Lehman failure, he guessed ~$200B net, NYU's Bruce Tuckman ~$80B, but later CFTC research under Tuckman found a Lehman failure would have triggered less than $9B in payouts.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Opacity, not exposure size, drove the 2008 panic.
insights.quote: would have triggered less than $9 billion a payout.

insights.claim: Giancarlo argues crises happen from opacity, and had the swaps been on a shared blockchain regulators would have known the true exposure and could have let Lehman fail, be bought, or be bailed out without a crisis.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Core institutional thesis: DLT as shared ledger reduces systemic risk.
insights.quote: crises happen when you have opacity because people don't know.

insights.claim: Giancarlo says he is certain the technology will take hold but uncertain whether democratic values can be encoded into it; China's digital yuan is a control instrument and Europe's digital euro a surveillance regime.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Privacy design is the main open variable in the digital-finance race.
insights.quote: I have every certainty that this technology is going to take hold. I don't have any certainty that we're going to be able to encode our democratic values in this digital future.

insights.claim: Giancarlo criticizes the GENIUS Act for imposing the Bank Secrecy Act on stablecoins, saying it brings government surveillance into the new financial system.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Stablecoins offer no privacy advantage; regulatory surveillance is a design constraint.
insights.quote: it imposed upon stable coins the very retrograde analog bank secrecy act, which has nothing to do with secrecy and everything to do with surveillance.

insights.claim: Giancarlo claims the US financial system is much closer to China's than anyone admits, completely surveilled since the 1970s BSA and 9/11, with the Supreme Court's third-party doctrine to blame, and warns the US is losing its advantage as a result.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Privacy policy may decide whether the US wins the DLT race.
insights.quote: our financial system today is much closer to Chinese system than anybody wants to admit.

insights.claim: Giancarlo calls the CBDC-vs-stablecoin privacy debate a false choice: stablecoins are fully subject to BSA surveillance, and a government issuer might even be constrained by the Fourth Amendment.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Challenges the US political consensus that stablecoins are the privacy-preserving alternative to a CBDC.
insights.quote: I reject the notion that CBDC is somehow an invasion of privacy and stable coins are somehow a protection of privacy. That's a completely false choice.

insights.claim: Giancarlo, chairman of the Digital Dollar Project, proposes that the dollar in any form must embed a probable-cause-plus-judicial-subpoena privacy standard, citing the IRS demand for Coinbase's customer data without suspicion as the wrong balance.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Privacy as dollar competitive advantage could become a policy agenda item.
insights.quote: Let's make the dollar the world's instrument of freedom and then people the world over will aspire to owning it.

insights.claim: Giancarlo cites an OCC report released that week saying the Biden administration used financial-transaction surveillance to debank people, including CEOs, for political or religious reasons.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo
insights.so_what: Debanking evidence strengthens the push for financial-privacy reform.

insights.claim: Host David notes that extreme on-chain transparency is showing up negatively in home invasions and kidnappings in France.
insights.speaker: David (host)
insights.so_what: Physical security risk from public ledgers is driving demand for on-chain privacy.
